```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                       fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 0.3)

# draws n full-width blank lines (margin to margin) for handwritten answers,
# as a single plot so spacing is deterministic; pair with fig.height = 0.3 * n
blank_lines <- function(n = 1) {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, n), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    segments(0, n - i + 0.5, 1, n - i + 0.5, lwd = 1)
  }
}

# reserves blank work space (no ruled lines) for equation manipulation /
# show-your-work; pair with fig.height set to however much room is needed
blank_space <- function() {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot.new()
}
```

```{r key-helpers, include=FALSE}
ans_col <- rgb(200, 0, 130, maxColorValue = 255)
# redraws blank_table() so cells flagged TRUE in `ans` use the answer color
blank_table <- function(headers, body, col_widths = NULL,
                        header_height = 0.35, row_height = 0.5,
                        cex = 0.95, bold_rows = integer(0), ans = NULL) {
  nc <- length(headers); nr <- length(body)
  if (is.null(col_widths)) col_widths <- rep(1, nc)
  col_widths <- col_widths / sum(col_widths)
  cx <- c(0, cumsum(col_widths))
  h_total <- header_height + nr * row_height
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0), family = "serif")
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, h_total), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
  y <- h_total
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  y <- y - header_height
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    y <- y - row_height
    segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = if (i == nr) 1.5 else 0.5,
             col = if (i == nr) "black" else "grey70")
  }
  for (v in cx) segments(v, 0, v, h_total, lwd = 1)
  yh <- h_total - header_height / 2
  for (j in seq_len(nc)) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yh, labels = headers[[j]], font = 2, cex = cex)
  y <- h_total - header_height
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    yc <- y - row_height / 2
    for (j in seq_len(nc)) {
      val <- body[[i]][[j]]
      is_ans <- !is.null(ans) && isTRUE(ans[[i]][[j]])
      if (!identical(val, "")) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yc, labels = val, cex = cex,
                                    font = if (i %in% bold_rows) 2 else 1,
                                    col = if (is_ans) ans_col else "black")
    }
    y <- y - row_height
  }
}
```

\ans{\textbf{Answer key.} Answers are in magenta.}


## Picking up where we left off

In Act 1 you dealt with *uncertainty about a single flagged image*.
Now set that aside -- assume genetic testing has confirmed the target
carnivore is present at a particular site (no more
classifier doubt to worry about). The new question is about *detection*:
even when the animal is really there, a camera doesn't catch it every
single night. Suppose, based on many past deployments at similar sites,
biologists estimate that on any given night there's a $p=0.3$
probability the camera captures at least one image of the animal,
independent from night to night (assuming it is genuinely there!).

## Part 1: Binomial by hand (individual, ~15 min)

A camera is deployed for $N=8$ nights.

**1a.** Why is "number of nights with a detection, out of 8" a
reasonable binomial random variable here? Name the assumptions the
binomial distribution requires, and say briefly why each one seems
plausible (or not) for this camera. Feel free to refer to the Bolker book here.

\ans{Fixed number of trials (8 nights, by design); two outcomes per night (detect or not); independent nights (plausible, but storms, malfunctions, or an animal revisiting a spot could link nights); constant $p$ (questionable: moon, weather, or the animal getting used to the camera can change it).}

**1b.** Using the binomial pmf, $P(X=k) = \binom{N}{k}p^k(1-p)^{N-k}$,
compute by hand the probability of exactly 3 detections in the 8
nights ($N=8$, $k=3$, $p=0.3$). Show your work.

\ans{$P(X = 3) = \binom{8}{3}(0.3)^3(0.7)^5 = 56 \times 0.027 \times 0.16807 \approx `r formatC(dbinom(3, 8, 0.3), format = "f", digits = 4)`$}

Below is the full distribution of detections across all 9 possible
outcomes ($k=0$ to $8$), for you to check your answer against and read
off the most likely outcome.

```{r binom-full, fig.height=3, fig.width=5}
barplot(dbinom(0:8, 8, 0.3), names.arg = 0:8, ylab = "Probability",
        xlab = "Number of detections (out of 8 nights)",
        main = "Binomial(N = 8, p = 0.3)")
```

**1c.** The mean of this distribution is $Np = 8\times0.3=2.4$, but the tallest bar (the mode) sits at a different whole number. Why can't the mode land exactly on the mean here? And what does the direction of the gap between them (mode below the mean, or above?) tell you about the shape of this distribution?

\ans{The mode is 2. Counts must be whole numbers, but the mean is an average and can fall between them. Mode below the mean means right skew: bounded at 0 with a longer upper tail pulling the mean up.}

## Part 2: Comparing to Poisson (individual, ~15-20 min)

A colleague suggests it would be simpler to just model detections with
a Poisson distribution instead, using the same mean,
$\lambda = 8\times0.3=2.4$. Below are two scenarios, each comparing a
binomial distribution against a Poisson with the same mean.

```{r pois-compare, fig.height=3.4, fig.width=6.5}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
barplot(dbinom(0:8, 8, 0.3), names.arg = 0:8, ylab = "Probability",
        main = "Scenario A:\nBinomial(N=8, p=0.3)", cex.main = 0.85)
barplot(dpois(0:8, 2.4), names.arg = 0:8, ylab = "Probability",
        main = "Scenario A:\nPoisson(lambda=2.4)", cex.main = 0.85)
```

```{r pois-compare2, fig.height=3.4, fig.width=6.5}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
barplot(dbinom(0:8, 100, 0.024), names.arg = 0:8, ylab = "Probability",
        main = "Scenario B:\nBinomial(N=100, p=0.024)", cex.main = 0.85)
barplot(dpois(0:8, 2.4), names.arg = 0:8, ylab = "Probability",
        main = "Scenario B:\nPoisson(lambda=2.4)", cex.main = 0.85)
```

**2a.** Look closely at both pairs of bar charts. In Scenario A, where specifically do the binomial and Poisson bars disagree most -- the center, the spread, or the tails? Does Scenario B show the same kind of disagreement, a different kind, or none at all?  

\ans{Scenario A: the spread. The binomial is taller in the middle (2 to 4); the Poisson puts more probability in both tails. Scenario B: almost no disagreement.}

**2b.** Compute the variance of each distribution by hand, using
$\text{Var} = Np(1-p)$ for the binomial and $\text{Var}=\lambda$ for
the Poisson.

\ans{A binomial: $8 \times 0.3 \times 0.7 = 1.68$. \quad B binomial: $100 \times 0.024 \times 0.976 = 2.3424$. \quad Poisson (both): $\lambda = 2.4$.}

**2c.** Does the pattern of variances you just computed explain what
you saw by eye in 2a?

\ans{Yes: in A the Poisson variance (2.4) is about 40\% larger than the binomial's (1.68), so it's wider; in B they're nearly equal (2.40 vs. 2.34).}

**2d.** Finish this rule of thumb in your own words: *"A Poisson
distribution is a good stand-in for a binomial distribution when..."*

\ans{...the number of trials is large and the probability per trial is small, so $1 - p \approx 1$ and $Np(1-p) \approx Np = \lambda$.}

**2e.** Back in the original 8-night scenario ($p=0.3$): name one
realistic reason the constant, independent per-night detection
probability assumption from 1a might be violated in the field.

\ans{E.g. a multi-night storm suppresses detections several nights in a row (breaks independence), or moon phase, season, or the animal learning to avoid the camera changes $p$.}

Compare your variances and rule of thumb from 2d with your group.
